title: Doxorubicin and cisplatin for osteosarcoma
context_label: Chemotherapy before and after surgery for osteosarcoma
indication_text: Chemotherapy before and after surgery for osteosarcoma
purpose: Chemotherapy treats osteosarcoma cells throughout the body, including cells too small to see on scans, alongside surgery intended to remove the visible cancer.
schedule_label: Doxorubicin days 1–3 and cisplatin day 1; six 21-day cycles
schedule_summary: Doxorubicin 25 mg/m² is given on days 1, 2 and 3; cisplatin 100 mg/m² on day 1. The reference course contains six 21-day cycles, usually three before surgery and three afterwards, with pathology review. Treatment dates and doses depend on recovery and the specialist plan.
administration_text: Doxorubicin is given through supervised intravenous access. Cisplatin is infused over 2 hours, with prescribed fluids and electrolytes before and afterwards. The full visit is longer than the drug infusion. A hospital fluid prescription is not a home drinking target.
monitoring_summary: Use the individual test cards below: each test has its own purpose and timing. Safety tests and tumour-response assessment answer different questions.

agents.name: Doxorubicin
agents.mechanism: Disrupts genetic material and the enzyme that repairs it
agents.explanation: Doxorubicin enters deoxyribonucleic acid, the genetic material called DNA, and interferes with topoisomerase II, an enzyme needed when cells copy and repair their genes. This damages tumour cells. Normal marrow, mouth and heart cells can also be injured.
agents.watch: Report fever, mouth ulcers, breathlessness, ankle swelling, palpitations or pain at the drip immediately.
risks: Low blood counts, serious infection or sepsis, anaemia and bleeding
Nausea, vomiting, mouth ulcers, appetite changes and diarrhoea
Hair loss, fatigue and skin or nail changes
Heart muscle damage or abnormal rhythm; damage can appear later and relates to lifetime anthracycline exposure
Severe local tissue damage if the drug leaks outside the vein; allergic reactions
Fertility and pregnancy harm; uncommon later blood cancers

agents.name: Cisplatin
agents.explanation: Cisplatin forms links within and between strands of DNA, the genetic material. These links stop cells copying their instructions normally. Kidney cells, the inner ear and nerves may also be injured, so prescribed fluids and organ checks are essential.
agents.watch: Report reduced urine, persistent vomiting, ringing ears, hearing changes, numbness or weakness before further treatment.
risks: Severe nausea and vomiting; dehydration can worsen kidney injury
Kidney damage and low magnesium, potassium or other electrolytes
Hearing loss or ringing in the ears, sometimes permanent
Numbness, tingling or weakness from nerve damage, sometimes lasting
Low blood counts, serious infection, anaemia and bleeding
Allergic reactions, infusion-site injury, fertility and pregnancy harm

anatomy: Report ringing ears or reduced hearing promptly. Hearing changes can persist.
Report ulcers, painful swallowing or difficulty eating and drinking early.
New breathlessness, chest pain, palpitations, faintness or swelling needs urgent assessment.
Report reduced urine or inability to drink. Kidney damage and electrolyte losses may need extra tests.
Fever, shaking chills, sudden illness or unusual bleeding requires immediate oncology advice.
Use prescribed anti-sickness support; report persistent vomiting, severe diarrhoea or difficulty drinking.
Hair and skin changes may occur. Report line-site pain, burning, swelling or a severe rash immediately.
Report tingling, numbness or weakness before another dose; these effects can affect walking or hand tasks.

monitoring_schedule.note: The national regimen, product information and individual clinical plan may require different tests. Your treating team writes the actual dates and reviews results before treatment.

monitoring_test_details.label: Full blood count
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Check infection-fighting cells, haemoglobin and platelets.
monitoring_test_details.timing: Before starting and before each 21-day cycle; repeat sooner for fever, bleeding or abnormal results.

monitoring_test_details.label: Kidney function and electrolytes
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Assess cisplatin kidney safety and identify magnesium or other electrolyte losses.
monitoring_test_details.timing: Before starting and before each cycle; additional checks accompany the prescribed hydration plan and reduced urine, dehydration or abnormal results.

monitoring_test_details.label: Liver tests
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Assess doxorubicin handling and detect liver injury.
monitoring_test_details.timing: Before starting and before each cycle; repeat when results or symptoms warrant.

monitoring_test_details.label: Heart tracing and heart imaging
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Assess cardiac risk alongside lifetime anthracycline exposure.
monitoring_test_details.timing: Heart tracing before starting. Heart ultrasound or multigated acquisition scan if age above 65 or clinically indicated in the source; repeat imaging when indicated by symptoms or risk. The linked doxorubicin product information additionally recommends baseline pumping-function imaging and repeats after approximately each accumulated 100 mg/m². The specialist team reconciles this with the national source and writes the cardiac monitoring schedule.

monitoring_test_details.label: Hearing assessment
monitoring_test_details.timing: Review symptoms before further cisplatin; formal audiology at baseline or later when clinically indicated. Report changes immediately.

monitoring_test_details.label: Nerve and symptom review
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Detect neuropathy and other treatment effects before more dosing.
monitoring_test_details.timing: At each treatment review and whenever numbness, weakness or other symptoms change.

monitoring_test_details.label: Surgery, pathology and response review
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Coordinate cancer control and postoperative treatment.
monitoring_test_details.timing: Review at the planned transition after three preoperative cycles and after surgery; scans and further reviews follow the consultant-set plan.

support.title: Preparation and support medicines
support.text: Bring the full medicine list, report infection or hearing/nerve changes, and confirm the anti-sickness and hydration prescription. Discuss heart history, all prior anthracyclines, fertility and the surgery plan. Cisplatin has high nausea/vomiting risk. Agree prevention and rescue anti-sickness medicines, prescribed hydration and electrolyte replacement. A separate white-cell growth-factor plan may be chosen for clinical need. Do not add diuretics or change fluid intake yourself.

support.title: Access and practical care
support.text: The team chooses appropriate intravenous access and explains its care. Report pain, burning, redness or swelling during treatment immediately. If a port or peripherally inserted central catheter is used, confirm dressing, flushing, infection precautions and eventual removal arrangements. Never change pump settings or disconnect an infusion yourself.

support.title: Fertility and pregnancy precautions
support.text: Discuss fertility preservation before treatment. Obtain written contraception, pregnancy and breastfeeding instructions for every medicine, including how long precautions continue after the final dose. Different medicines have different requirements. Contact oncology promptly if pregnancy is possible. Children and young people need age-appropriate information, assent and the applicable parent or guardian consent process.

support.title: Your wider treatment plan
support.text: A specialist sarcoma multidisciplinary team plans chemotherapy together with complete removal of the tumour and any other resectable disease sites. The operation, reconstruction, rehabilitation and pathology review are central parts of the plan. Radiotherapy can be considered when surgery is not feasible or margins are inadequate; it is not automatically added to every osteosarcoma course.

items.title: General chemotherapy risks
items.text: Discuss low blood counts with serious infection or sepsis, anaemia and bleeding; nausea or vomiting; mouth soreness, appetite or taste changes, diarrhoea or constipation; fatigue, hair, nail and skin changes; changes in sexual wellbeing; allergic reactions and intravenous-line complications; blood clots, including clots in the legs or lungs; fertility, pregnancy and breastfeeding effects; and the possibility of lasting organ injury, rare later cancers or death from serious treatment complications. The likelihood and severity differ between medicines and people. Read this general discussion together with every medicine-specific risk.

evidence.title: European Osteosarcoma Intergroup historical randomised comparison
evidence.summary: A historical randomised study of operable, nonmetastatic osteosarcoma found similar observed five-year survival and progression outcomes with six courses of doxorubicin/cisplatin and a much longer multidrug course. More patients completed the shorter course.
evidence.intro: A historical randomised study of operable, nonmetastatic osteosarcoma found similar observed five-year survival and progression outcomes with six courses of doxorubicin/cisplatin and a much longer multidrug course. More patients completed the shorter course.
evidence.caveat: The comparator was a historical 44-week regimen. This is not a modern direct comparison against methotrexate/doxorubicin/cisplatin and does not prove equivalence to all current regimens or predict an individual outcome.
evidence.interpretation: The comparator was a historical 44-week regimen. This is not a modern direct comparison against methotrexate/doxorubicin/cisplatin and does not prove equivalence to all current regimens or predict an individual outcome.

questions.q: What is the treatment trying to do?
questions.a: Chemotherapy treats osteosarcoma cells throughout the body, including cells too small to see on scans, alongside surgery intended to remove the visible cancer. A specialist sarcoma multidisciplinary team plans chemotherapy together with complete removal of the tumour and any other resectable disease sites. The operation, reconstruction, rehabilitation and pathology review are central parts of the plan. Radiotherapy can be considered when surgery is not feasible or margins are inadequate; it is not automatically added to every osteosarcoma course.

Doxorubicin 25 mg/m² is given on days 1, 2 and 3; cisplatin 100 mg/m² on day 1. The reference course contains six 21-day cycles, usually three before surgery and three afterwards, with pathology review. Treatment dates and doses depend on recovery and the specialist plan.

questions.q: Does a delay mean treatment has failed?
questions.a: No. Blood counts, organ function and symptoms can make a delay or dose change safer. Your team decides whether and when to give the next dose.

questions.q: Who do I contact if unwell?
questions.a: Use your verified oncology daytime or out-of-hours number. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Severe symptoms require 112/999.

questions.q: Can treatment restart when a blood test improves?
questions.a: Only when the treating team confirms a new plan. A previous serious reaction, stopped medicine or required protective treatment still matters.
